newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Will EMU be purchased at any price?.
newsitem.headline: Will EMU be purchased at any price?.

text.p: France's lurch to the political left has raised profound doubts over the willingness of European leaders to push ahead with a single currency and fuelled speculation that a delay might realistically be considered.

Analysts say the stunning French Socialist victory has not only called into question France's ability to adhere to the budgetary rigours of a single currency -- it has also rekindled doubts over the all important Franco-German political axis.

"I think that Franco-German relations will be much tougher because it looks as though we will get a euro which has become a relative currency and not the absolute one the Germans wanted," said one German political analyst.

French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said he would not consider implementing further austerity measures ahead of the introduction of the euro in 1999 and has argued for a more flexible interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty's criteria.

The new position, a striking contrast with that of the ousted centre-right government, has opened the door to the possiblity of a broad and relatively weak euro, incorporating many more countries than envisaged only a few months ago.

A second worry among analysts is that the political sea change in France, coupled with Britain's new Labour government and the broad undercurrent of popular discontent over Europe's high unemployment, might cause Germany to question whether the whole project is really worth it.

Most believe German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has not reached the point where he would put domestic troubles ahead of his grand vision of European unity. To turn back now would be devastating, not only for the chances of ever forging a single currency but for EU integration across all political fronts.

Yet if the latest verdict from France says anything with absolute clarity it is that the policies both Germany and France have pursued in recent years may have run their course among those who ultimately matter.

"Kohl must ask himself about the fact that his policy has been rejected by quite a majority of French voters and if you voted today in Germany the outcome would be the same," said one EU monetary official.

In Germany, the degree of political disorientation has reached an almost fever pitch, prompted in part by the government's plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves in order to plug an enormous revenue shortfall.

With the Bundesbank having rejected the proposal and Bonn poised to slip it through the German parliament, the episode has unleashed a war of words between the two camps, putting the credibility of Germany's central bank at centre stage.

Analysts say the options for European leaders at this point are still basically two -- a broad euro with lots of members or no euro at all. The former is considered by most EU officials as the most likely scenario.
"These are all signs of a willingness to respect the deadline," said one senior EU official.
"There is no way back. There is too much investment -- politically, economically and financially. I think a delay is more and more improbable."
But among private forecasters the odds of a postponement have risen considerably, and many are now seriously entertaining the notion.

"A rational solution might be to decide to pause for further thought and consider postponement," said John Arrowsmith, an economist with the National Institute for Social and Economic Research in London.
The reasons for this are several, not least the view that there may be limits to which Germany will be prepared to purchase a currency that has become increasingly politicised.

Although no one ever doubted that economic and monetary union was foremost a political project, analysts say the events over the past few weeks have swung too far towards this direction, risking the credibility that a new and untested currency would need.
